  title: Next Steps

The `prefetch` route segment config controls how a segment is prefetched during client-side navigation. By default, the framework manages the strategy based on the app's [`partialPrefetching`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching) setting. To override per segment, set this export to one of the values below.

> **Good to know**:
>
> - The `prefetch` export only works when [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled.
> - `prefetch` cannot be used when the segment is a Client Component.
> - The meaningful values to set are `'partial'` and `'force-disabled'`. `'auto'` is the default and is equivalent to omitting the export; don't write `prefetch = 'auto'` explicitly.

The `prefetch` route segment config controls how a segment is prefetched during client-side navigation. By default, the framework manages the strategy based on the app's [`partialPrefetching`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching) setting. To override per segment, set this export to one of the values below.

> **Good to know**:
>
> - The `prefetch` export only works when [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled.
> - `prefetch` cannot be used when the segment is a Client Component.
> - The meaningful values to set are `'partial'` and `'force-disabled'`. `'auto'` is the default and is equivalent to omitting the export; don't write `prefetch = 'auto'` explicitly.

The `instant` route segment config controls how Next.js validates whether a navigation into this segment would produce an instant UI.

Next.js uses prefetching to preload navigations for all in-app links on the current page. However, client-side data fetching or partially prerendered results from the server can lead to navigations that don't update the UI immediately. To help you build fast-feeling navigations, `instant` lets you tell Next.js what to expect from navigations through the configured segment. For instance, you can indicate that navigations into this segment should produce a UI that renders instantly without waiting on any externally loaded data. You can also indicate that navigations aren't expected to be instant.

When a segment is configured to expect an instant UI, Next.js surfaces any code in your application that would block the navigation from updating the UI immediately. See the [Instant Navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) for an end-to-end walkthrough.

> **Good to know**:

---
title: instant
description: API reference for the instant route segment config.
related:
  title: Next Steps
  description: Learn how to use instant navigations in practice.
  links:
    - app/guides/instant-navigation
    - app/getting-started/caching
    - app/getting-started/revalidating
    - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache
---

The `instant` route segment config controls how Next.js validates whether a navigation into this segment would produce an instant UI.

Next.js uses prefetching to preload navigations for all in-app links on the current page. However, client-side data fetching or partially prerendered results from the server can lead to navigations that don't update the UI immediately. To help you build fast-feeling navigations, `instant` lets you tell Next.js what to expect from navigations through the configured segment. For instance, you can indicate that navigations into this segment should produce a UI that renders instantly without waiting on any externally loaded data. You can also indicate that navigations aren't expected to be instant.

When a segment is configured to expect an instant UI, Next.js surfaces any code in your application that would block the navigation from updating the UI immediately. See the [Instant Navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) for an end-to-end walkthrough.

> **Good to know**:

00441|   )
00442| }
00443| ```
00444| 
00445| ### `as`
00446| 
00447| Optional decorator for the path that will be shown in the browser URL bar. Before Next.js 9.5.3 this was used for dynamic routes, check our [previous docs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v9.5.2/docs/api-reference/next/link.md#dynamic-routes) to see how it worked.
00448| 
00449| When this path differs from the one provided in `href` the previous `href`/`as` behavior is used as shown in the [previous docs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v9.5.2/docs/api-reference/next/link.md#dynamic-routes).
00450| 
00451| </PagesOnly>
00452| 
00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.
00504| 
00505| ### `transitionTypes`
00506| 
00507| <AppOnly>
00508| 
00509| A list of transition types to apply to the navigation. These types are passed to [`React.addTransitionType`](https://react.dev/reference/react/addTransitionType) inside the navigation transition, enabling [`<ViewTransition>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) components to apply different animations based on the type of navigation.
00510| 
00511| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00512| import Link from 'next/link'
00513| 
00514| export default function Page() {
00515|   return (
00516|     <Link href="/about" transitionTypes={['slide-in']}>
00517|       About
00518|     </Link>
00519|   )
00520| }
00521| ```
00522| 
00523| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00524| import Link from 'next/link'
00525| 
00526| export default function Page() {
00527|   return (
00528|     <Link href="/about" transitionTypes={['slide-in']}>
00529|       About
00530|     </Link>
00531|   )
00532| }
00533| ```

00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. 00546| 
00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher

00553|   slug: string

00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>

00687| ### Scrolling to an `id`

00689| If you'd like to scroll to a specific `id` on navigation, you can append your URL with a `#` hash link or just pass a hash link to the `href` prop. This is possible since `<Link>` renders to an `<a>` element.

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.
00852| 
00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.
00854| 
00855| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00856| import Link from 'next/link'
00857| 
00858| export default function Page() {
00859|   return (
00860|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00861|       Disables scrolling to the top
00862|     </Link>
00863|   )
00864| }
00865| ```
00866| 
00867| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00868| import Link from 'next/link'
00869| 
00870| export default function Page() {
00871|   return (
00872|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00873|       Disables scrolling to the top
00874|     </Link>
00875|   )
00876| }
00877| ```
00878| 
00879| Using `router.push()` or `router.replace()`:
00880| 
00881| ```jsx
00882| // useRouter
00883| import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
00884| 
00885| const router = useRouter()
00886| 
00887| router.push('/dashboard', { scroll: false })
00888| ```
00889| 
00890| </AppOnly>
00891| 
00892| <PagesOnly>
00893| 
00894| The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page. When there is a hash defined it will scroll to the specific id, like a normal `<a>` tag. To prevent scrolling to the top / hash `scroll={false}` can be added to `Link`:

00904|   )
00905| }
00906| ```

00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers
00923| 
00924| Because Next.js skips sticky and fixed positioned elements when finding the scroll target, content may end up behind a sticky header after navigation. For example, if your layout has a sticky header:
00925| 
00926| ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
00927| import './globals.css'
00928| 
00929| export default function RootLayout({
00930|   children,
00931| }: {
00932|   children: React.ReactNode
00933| }) {
00934|   return (
00935|     <html lang="en">
00936|       <body>
00937|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00938|           {/* Navigation */}
00939|         </header>
00940|         {children}
00941|       </body>
00942|     </html>
00943|   )
00944| }
00945| ```
00946| 
00947| ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
00948| import './globals.css'
00949| 
00950| export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
00951|   return (
00952|     <html lang="en">
00953|       <body>
00954|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00955|           {/* Navigation */}
00956|         </header>
00957|         {children}
00958|       </body>
00959|     </html>
00960|   )
00961| }
00962| ```
00963| 
00964| You can account for its height using [`scroll-padding-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-padding-top) on the scroll container:
00965| 
00966| ```css filename="app/globals.css"
00967| html {
00968|   scroll-padding-top: 64px; /* Match the height of your sticky header */
00969| }
00970| ```
00971| 
00972| This is a browser CSS property that offsets scroll-based positioning. It applies whenever Next.js uses the native [`scrollIntoView()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollIntoView) API, including hash fragment (`#id`) navigation. Alternatively, you can use [`scroll-margin-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-margin-top) on individual target elements instead of setting a global offset.
00973| 
00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979| 
00980| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00981| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00982| 
00983| export function proxy(request: Request) {
00984|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
00985|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
00986|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
00987|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
00988|     } else {
00989|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
00990|     }
00991|   }
00992| }
00993| ```
00994| 
00995| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00996| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00997| 
00998| export function proxy(request) {
00999|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
01000|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
01001|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
01002|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
01003|     } else {
01004|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
01005|     }
01006|   }
01007| }
01008| ```
01009| 
01010| In this case, you would want to use the following code in your `<Link />` component:
01011| 
01012| <AppOnly>
01013| 
01014| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher

01022|   const path = isAuthed ? '/auth/dashboard' : '/public/dashboard'
01023|   return (
01024|     <Link as="/dashboard" href={path}>
01025|       Dashboard
01026|     </Link>
01027|   )
01028| }
01029| ```
01030|

01092| ### Blocking navigation
01093| 
01094| You can use the `onNavigate` prop to block navigation when certain conditions are met, such as when a form has unsaved changes. When you need to block navigation across multiple components in your app (like preventing navigation from any link while a form is being edited), React Context provides a clean way to share this blocking state. First, create a context to track the navigation blocking state:
01095| 
01096| ```tsx filename="app/contexts/navigation-blocker.tsx" switcher
01097| 'use client'
01098| 
01099| import { createContext, useState, useContext } from 'react'
01100| 
01101| interface NavigationBlockerContextType {
01102|   isBlocked: boolean
01103|   setIsBlocked: (isBlocked: boolean) => void
01104| }
01105| 
01106| export const NavigationBlockerContext =
01107|   createContext<NavigationBlockerContextType>({
01108|     isBlocked: false,
01109|     setIsBlocked: () => {},
01110|   })
01111| 
01112| export function NavigationBlockerProvider({
01113|   children,
01114| }: {
01115|   children: React.ReactNode
01116| }) {

title: Link Component
description: Enable fast client-side navigation with the built-in `next/link` component.
---

{/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `<PagesOnly>Content</PagesOnly>` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */}

`<Link>` is a React component that extends the HTML `<a>` element to provide [prefetching](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#prefetching) and client-side navigation between routes. It is the primary way to navigate between routes in Next.js.

Basic usage:

<AppOnly>

```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Page() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

00411|       </Link>

00447| Optional decorator for the path that will be shown in the browser URL bar. Before Next.js 9.5.3 this was used for dynamic routes, check our [previous docs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v9.5.2/docs/api-reference/next/link.md#dynamic-routes) to see how it worked.

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.
00504|

00515|   return (

00517|       About
00518|     </Link>

00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. For example, to generate a list of blog posts:
00546| 
00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher

00552|   title: string
00553|   slug: string
00554| }
00555| 
00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>
00563|       ))}

00565|   )

00687| ### Scrolling to an `id`
00688| 
00689| If you'd like to scroll to a specific `id` on navigation, you can append your URL with a `#` hash link or just pass a hash link to the `href` prop. This is possible since `<Link>` renders to an `<a>` element.

00691| ```jsx

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.
00852| 
00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.
00854| 
00855| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00856| import Link from 'next/link'
00857| 
00858| export default function Page() {
00859|   return (
00860|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00861|       Disables scrolling to the top
00862|     </Link>
00863|   )
00864| }
00865| ```
00866| 
00867| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00868| import Link from 'next/link'
00869| 
00870| export default function Page() {
00871|   return (
00872|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00873|       Disables scrolling to the top
00874|     </Link>
00875|   )
00876| }
00877| ```
00878| 
00879| Using `router.push()` or `router.replace()`:
00880| 
00881| ```jsx
00882| // useRouter
00883| import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
00884| 
00885| const router = useRouter()
00886| 
00887| router.push('/dashboard', { scroll: false })
00888| ```
00889| 
00890| </AppOnly>
00891| 
00892| <PagesOnly>
00893| 
00894| The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page. When there is a hash defined it will scroll to the specific id, like a normal `<a>` tag. To prevent scrolling to the top / hash `scroll={false}` can be added to `Link`:

00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers
00923| 
00924| Because Next.js skips sticky and fixed positioned elements when finding the scroll target, content may end up behind a sticky header after navigation. For example, if your layout has a sticky header:
00925| 
00926| ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
00927| import './globals.css'
00928| 
00929| export default function RootLayout({
00930|   children,
00931| }: {
00932|   children: React.ReactNode
00933| }) {
00934|   return (
00935|     <html lang="en">
00936|       <body>
00937|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00938|           {/* Navigation */}
00939|         </header>
00940|         {children}
00941|       </body>
00942|     </html>
00943|   )
00944| }
00945| ```
00946| 
00947| ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
00948| import './globals.css'
00949| 
00950| export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
00951|   return (
00952|     <html lang="en">
00953|       <body>
00954|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00955|           {/* Navigation */}
00956|         </header>
00957|         {children}
00958|       </body>
00959|     </html>
00960|   )
00961| }
00962| ```
00963| 
00964| You can account for its height using [`scroll-padding-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-padding-top) on the scroll container:
00965| 
00966| ```css filename="app/globals.css"
00967| html {
00968|   scroll-padding-top: 64px; /* Match the height of your sticky header */
00969| }
00970| ```
00971| 
00972| This is a browser CSS property that offsets scroll-based positioning. It applies whenever Next.js uses the native [`scrollIntoView()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollIntoView) API, including hash fragment (`#id`) navigation. Alternatively, you can use [`scroll-margin-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-margin-top) on individual target elements instead of setting a global offset.
00973| 
00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979| 
00980| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00981| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00982| 
00983| export function proxy(request: Request) {
00984|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
00985|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
00986|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
00987|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
00988|     } else {
00989|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
00990|     }
00991|   }
00992| }
00993| ```
00994| 
00995| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00996| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00997| 
00998| export function proxy(request) {
00999|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
01000|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
01001|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
01002|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
01003|     } else {
01004|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
01005|     }
01006|   }
01007| }
01008| ```
01009| 
01010| In this case, you would want to use the following code in your `<Link />` component:

01022|   const path = isAuthed ? '/auth/dashboard' : '/public/dashboard'
01023|   return (
01024|     <Link as="/dashboard" href={path}>
01025|       Dashboard
01026|     </Link>
01027|   )
01028| }
01029| ```

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.
00504|

00515|   return (

00517|       About
00518|     </Link>
00519|   )
00520| }

00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. 00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher

00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>

00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.
00852| 
00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.
00854| 
00855| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00856| import Link from 'next/link'
00857| 
00858| export default function Page() {
00859|   return (
00860|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00861|       Disables scrolling to the top
00862|     </Link>
00863|   )
00864| }
00865| ```
00866| 
00867| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00868| import Link from 'next/link'
00869| 
00870| export default function Page() {
00871|   return (
00872|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00873|       Disables scrolling to the top
00874|     </Link>
00875|   )
00876| }
00877| ```
00878| 
00879| Using `router.push()` or `router.replace()`:
00880| 
00881| ```jsx
00882| // useRouter
00883| import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
00884| 
00885| const router = useRouter()
00886| 
00887| router.push('/dashboard', { scroll: false })
00888| ```
00889| 
00890| </AppOnly>
00891| 
00892| <PagesOnly>
00893| 
00894| The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page. When there is a hash defined it will scroll to the specific id, like a normal `<a>` tag. To prevent scrolling to the top / hash `scroll={false}` can be added to `Link`:

00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers
00923| 
00924| Because Next.js skips sticky and fixed positioned elements when finding the scroll target, content may end up behind a sticky header after navigation. For example, if your layout has a sticky header:
00925| 
00926| ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
00927| import './globals.css'
00928| 
00929| export default function RootLayout({
00930|   children,
00931| }: {
00932|   children: React.ReactNode
00933| }) {
00934|   return (
00935|     <html lang="en">
00936|       <body>
00937|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00938|           {/* Navigation */}
00939|         </header>
00940|         {children}
00941|       </body>
00942|     </html>
00943|   )
00944| }
00945| ```
00946| 
00947| ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
00948| import './globals.css'
00949| 
00950| export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
00951|   return (
00952|     <html lang="en">
00953|       <body>
00954|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00955|           {/* Navigation */}
00956|         </header>
00957|         {children}
00958|       </body>
00959|     </html>
00960|   )
00961| }
00962| ```
00963| 
00964| You can account for its height using [`scroll-padding-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-padding-top) on the scroll container:
00965| 
00966| ```css filename="app/globals.css"
00967| html {
00968|   scroll-padding-top: 64px; /* Match the height of your sticky header */
00969| }
00970| ```
00971| 
00972| This is a browser CSS property that offsets scroll-based positioning. It applies whenever Next.js uses the native [`scrollIntoView()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollIntoView) API, including hash fragment (`#id`) navigation. Alternatively, you can use [`scroll-margin-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-margin-top) on individual target elements instead of setting a global offset.
00973| 
00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979| 
00980| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00981| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00982| 
00983| export function proxy(request: Request) {
00984|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
00985|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
00986|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
00987|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
00988|     } else {
00989|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
00990|     }
00991|   }
00992| }
00993| ```
00994| 
00995| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00996| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00997| 
00998| export function proxy(request) {
00999|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
01000|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
01001|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
01002|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
01003|     } else {
01004|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
01005|     }
01006|   }
01007| }
01008| ```
01009| 
01010| In this case, you would want to use the following code in your `<Link />` component:
01011| 
01012| <AppOnly>
01013| 
01014| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
01015| 'use client'
01016| 
01017| import Link from 'next/link'
01018| import useIsAuthed from './hooks/useIsAuthed' // Your auth hook
01019|

`<Link>` is a React component that extends the HTML `<a>` element to provide [prefetching](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#prefetching) and client-side navigation between routes. It is the primary way to navigate between routes in Next.js.

import Link from 'next/link'

  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

00002| title: Ensuring instant navigations
00003| description: Learn how to structure your app to prefetch and prerender more content, providing instant page loads and client navigations.
00004| nav_title: Instant navigation
00005| related:
00006|   title: Learn more
00007|   description: Explore the full instant API, caching, and revalidation.
00008|   links:
00009|     - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/instant

00014| ---
00015| 
00016| This guide walks through understanding instant navigations, writing a route that navigates instantly, visualizing what's in the initial UI, and locking the behavior in with end-to-end tests.
00017| 
00018| ## What "instant" means
00019| 
00020| A navigation is **instant** when the browser can start rendering the new page the moment the user clicks, with static, cached, and fallback content showing up right away, while the server streams the remaining content into its fallbacks.
00021| 
00022| > **Good to know:** This definition assumes caches are warm. Cold caches still require the server to compute the cached result once, so the first navigation to a route may still wait.
00023| 
00024| A direct visit and a client navigation to the same route can produce different initial UI. **Direct visits** get the [**static shell**](/docs/app/glossary#static-shell) as HTML, typically from a CDN. **Client navigations** only re-render below the layout the current and destination routes share, so the fallback UI defined by a `<Suspense>` boundary above that point can't be used during the transition.
00025| 
00026| Whether the new page appears instantly depends on the `<Suspense>` boundaries and caching present below the shared layout.
00027| 
00028| <details>
00029| <summary>Why page loads and client navigations produce different initial UI</summary>
00030| 
00031| On a page load, the entire page renders from the document root. Every component runs on the server, and anything that suspends is caught by the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary in the full tree.
00032| 
00033| On a client navigation between `/store/shoes` and `/store/hats`, only the components below the `/store` layout re-render. A `<Suspense>` boundary in the root layout covers everything on a page load, but on this navigation, it sits above the re-render scope and does not trigger.
00034| 
00035| This is also why client-side hooks behave differently. `useSearchParams()` suspends during server rendering because search params are not available at build time. But on a client navigation, the router already has the params from the URL and the hook resolves synchronously. The same component can render immediately on a client navigation but sit behind a fallback on a page load.
00036| 
00037| </details>
00038| 
00039| With `prefetch={true}`, per-link prefetching resolves a link's URL data (`searchParams` and `params`) before navigation. First make the route instant with its App Shell. Per-link prefetching cannot fix a route that blocks without it. See [Optimizing prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) for the patterns.
00040| 
00041| ## Quick start
00042| 
00043| Getting the most out of Instant Navigation requires enabling [Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components) and [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching), then following the [validation errors](#validate-instant-navigation) that appear:
00044| 
00045| ```ts filename="next.config.ts"
00046| import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
00047| 
00048| const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
00049|   cacheComponents: true,
00050|   partialPrefetching: true,
00051| }
00052| 
00053| export default nextConfig
00054| ```
00055| 
00056| To help you automate this process with an agent, there's a Skill for each part, [next-cache-components-adoption](https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-cache-components-adoption) and [next-partial-prefetching-adoption](https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-partial-prefetching-adoption). If you'd like to enable everything, give your agent this prompt:
00057| 
00058| ```prompt
00059| Adopt Cache Components and Partial Prefetching in this app so its navigations become instant. There is a Skill for each migration.
00060| 
00061| 1. Before you change anything, explain to me in plain terms what Instant Navigation is and what adopting it will change.
00062| 
00063| 2. Install the Skills you need, then verify your changes against a running dev server with next-dev-loop and agent-browser as you go:
00064|    - next-cache-components-adoption: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-cache-components-adoption
00065|    - next-partial-prefetching-adoption: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-partial-prefetching-adoption
00066|    - next-dev-loop: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-dev-loop
00067| 
00068| 3. Each Skill leaves decisions to me, like how much of the work lands in each pull request. Put those questions to me and wait for my answers instead of deciding on my behalf. Adopt Cache Components first, then Partial Prefetching, following the workflow each Skill lays out. Don't rush to a passing build.
00069| 
00070| 4. When you finish a step, show me a table of the routes you touched and what changed on each, and talk me through what it means for the app. Keep it to the outcome, not the implementation details.
00071| ```
00072| 
00073| The rest of this guide covers the tools these migrations use, walks a navigation that blocks to instant, inspects what lands in the initial UI, and locks the result in with end-to-end tests.
00074| 
00075| ## The tools
00076| 
00077| ### Build the static shell
00078| 
00079| With Cache Components, **caching directives** (`"use cache"` and its variants) assign a lifetime to an async function's result, which is what lets Next.js include it in the static shell.
00080| 
00081| > **Good to know:** [`"use cache: private"`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private) is a variant for caching functions that read runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()`. The result is cached in the browser only, not on the server. **It can't be part of the static shell.** See [`"use cache: private"`](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching#use-cache-private) in the Optimizing prefetching guide for how it pairs with prefetching.
00082| 
00083| **`<Suspense>`** declares fallback UI for parts of the tree that read uncached data or runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()`; the content streams into the fallback when it resolves.
00084| 
00085| > **Good to know:** A fallback may access `cookies()`, `headers()`, or the full URL. At build time, the fallback itself suspends, and a `<Suspense>` boundary further up the tree is needed. For a link with `prefetch={true}`, [per-link prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) makes URL data available before navigation, so the fallback can become part of the prefetched UI. Cached values like timestamps or data fetches can sit directly inside the fallback.
00086| 
00087| Next.js can also generate an [**App Shell**](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) per route, which renders during client navigations while remaining content streams. Partial Prefetching uses the App Shell as the default `<Link>` prefetch. A link with `prefetch={true}` can also resolve cached content that depends on that link's URL data.
00088| 
00089| ### Prefetch URL data for a link
00090| 
00091| Under [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching), each visible `<Link>` prefetches the destination's App Shell by default. Links to the same route share one App Shell instead of triggering a separate App Shell request for each link.
00092| 
00093| To prefetch the page content alongside the shell for a specific link, set [`prefetch={true}`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#prefetch):
00094| 
00095| ```tsx
00096| <Link href="/checkout" prefetch>
00097|   Checkout
00098| </Link>
00099| ```

00021|

00025| 
00026| Whether the new page appears instantly depends on the `<Suspense>` boundaries and caching present below the shared layout.
00027| 
00028| <details>
00029| <summary>Why page loads and client navigations produce different initial UI</summary>
00030| 
00031| On a page load, the entire page renders from the document root. Every component runs on the server, and anything that suspends is caught by the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary in the full tree.
00032| 
00033| On a client navigation between `/store/shoes` and `/store/hats`, only the components below the `/store` layout re-render. A `<Suspense>` boundary in the root layout covers everything on a page load, but on this navigation, it sits above the re-render scope and does not trigger.
00034| 
00035| This is also why client-side hooks behave differently. `useSearchParams()` suspends during server rendering because search params are not available at build time. But on a client navigation, the router already has the params from the URL and the hook resolves synchronously. The same component can render immediately on a client navigation but sit behind a fallback on a page load.
00036| 
00037| </details>
00038| 
00039| With `prefetch={true}`, per-link prefetching resolves a link's URL data (`searchParams` and `params`) before navigation. First make the route instant with its App Shell. Per-link prefetching cannot fix a route that blocks without it. See [Optimizing prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) for the patterns.
00040| 
00041| ## Quick start
00042| 
00043| Getting the most out of Instant Navigation requires enabling [Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components) and [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching), then following the [validation errors](#validate-instant-navigation) that appear:

00046| import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
00047| 
00048| const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
00049|   cacheComponents: true,
00050|   partialPrefetching: true,
00051| }
00052| 
00053| export default nextConfig
00054| ```

00059| Adopt Cache Components and Partial Prefetching in this app so its navigations become instant. There is a Skill for each migration.

00061| 1. Before you change anything, explain to me in plain terms what Instant Navigation is and what adopting it will change.
00062|

00064|    - next-cache-components-adoption: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-cache-components-adoption
00065|    - next-partial-prefetching-adoption: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-partial-prefetching-adoption

00067|

00071| ```

00074| 
00075| ## The tools

00078|

00081| > **Good to know:** [`"use cache: private"`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private) is a variant for caching functions that read runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()`. Prefetching downloads a route's JavaScript, CSS, and RSC payload before the user navigates to it, so the router can render the next route without waiting for a round trip. The [Prefetching guide](/docs/app/guides/prefetching) covers what the App Router prefetches by default.

title: unstable_prefetch
description: API Reference for the unstable_prefetch function, which keeps a subtree out of a route's App Shell so it renders on a per-link prefetch or a navigation.
version: experimental
related:
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/navigation
    - app/api-reference/functions/connection
    - app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching
    - app/api-reference/functions/io
    - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching
    - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents
---

Calling `await unstable_prefetch()` defers the code below it to a per-link prefetch or a navigation, instead of rendering it in the route's [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell). The fallback of the nearest [`<Suspense>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) boundary takes its place in the shell, and the deferred content renders once one of those happens.

It is meant to defer content that the App Shell would otherwise render, typically content that depends on session data and is expensive to generate. During a build-time prerender nothing is deferred, so content below `unstable_prefetch()` is prerendered as usual.

## Usage

title: unstable_prefetch
description: API Reference for the unstable_prefetch function, which keeps a subtree out of a route's App Shell so it renders on a per-link prefetch or a navigation.
version: experimental

Calling `await unstable_prefetch()` defers the code below it to a per-link prefetch or a navigation, instead of rendering it in the route's [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell). It is meant to defer content that the App Shell would otherwise render, typically content that depends on session data and is expensive to generate. During a build-time prerender nothing is deferred, so content below `unstable_prefetch()` is prerendered as usual.

## Usage

title: unstable_navigation
description: API Reference for the unstable_navigation function, which keeps a subtree out of a route's prefetches so it renders when the user navigates.
version: experimental
related:

---

Calling `await unstable_navigation()` defers the code below it to the navigation, instead of rendering it when a link to the route is prefetched. The fallback of the nearest [`<Suspense>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) boundary takes its place in the prefetch, and the deferred content renders when the user navigates.

It is meant to defer content that a prefetch would otherwise render, even content that would sit in the App Shell, typically because it depends on session data or URL data and is expensive to generate. During a build-time prerender nothing is deferred, so content below `unstable_navigation()` is prerendered as usual.

## Usage

/**
 * OpenCode in-sandbox runner.
 *
 * This file is shipped INTO the sandbox by the orchestrator and executed there as
 * `node __agent_eval__/run.mjs '<AgentRunInput JSON>'`. It is intentionally
 * ZERO-DEPENDENCY (only `node:*` builtins) because the sandbox only has the
 * fixture's own deps + the installed `opencode` CLI — it cannot import anything
 * from the @vercel/agent-eval package.
 *
 * Dual mode:
 *   - runnable: invoked directly → reads argv, runs the agent, writes the result
 *     file + prints a status line, exits 0.
 *   - importable: `import { runAgent } from './run.mjs'` → returns a RunnerResult
 *     (no file write, no exit). This is what a future in-sandbox judge reuses.
 *
 * The pure helpers below are exported (not just `runAgent`) so they can be
 * unit-tested directly — the same code the sandbox runs (see opencode.test.ts).
 */

import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';

00065|  *
00066|  * Everything else passes through untouched: native-default runs (no override —
00067|  * consumers already treat `vercel/google/gemini-3-pro-preview` as canonical),
00068|  * callers that already speak OpenCode's namespace (`vercel/...` requested), and
00069|  * extraProviders runs (their providerID isn't `vercel`).
00070|  *
00071|  * @param {string|undefined} observedModel
00072|  * @param {{model?:string, extra?:Record<string,unknown>}} input
00073|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00074|  */
00075| export function normalizeObservedModel(observedModel, input) {
00076|   if (!observedModel) {
00077|     return observedModel;
00078|   }
00079|   const cliModel = input.extra?.cliModel;
00080|   const hostPrefixed = typeof cliModel === 'string' && cliModel !== input.model;
00081|   if (hostPrefixed && observedModel.startsWith('vercel/')) {
00082|     return observedModel.slice('vercel/'.length);
00083|   }
00084|   return observedModel;
00085| }
00086| 
00087| /**
00088|  * Extract transcript from OpenCode JSON output.
00089|  * When run with --format json, OpenCode outputs JSON events to stdout.
00090|  * Preserved verbatim from the old adapter.
00091|  *
00092|  * @param {string|undefined|null} output
00093|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00094|  */
00095| export function extractTranscriptFromOutput(output) {
00096|   if (!output || !output.trim()) {
00097|     return undefined;
00098|   }
00099| 
00100|   // The --format json output contains JSON events, one per line.
00101|   // Filter to only include lines that look like JSON objects.
00102|   const lines = output.split('\n').filter((line) => {
00103|     const trimmed = line.trim();
00104|     return trimmed.startsWith('{') && trimmed.endsWith('}');
00105|   });
00106| 
00107|   if (lines.length === 0) {
00108|     return undefined;
00109|   }
00110| 
00111|   return lines.join('\n');
00112| }
00113| 
00114| /**
00115|  * Scrape the OpenCode printed logs for the primary build model.
00116|  * Works on OpenCode <= 1.16.x, whose INFO log lines carry providerID/modelID.
00117|  * Preserved verbatim from the old adapter.
00118|  *
00119|  * @param {string} output
00120|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00121|  */
00122| export function extractObservedModelFromOpenCodeOutput(output) {
00123|   let observedModel;
00124| 
00125|   for (const line of output.split('\n')) {
00126|     if (!line.includes('service=llm') || !line.includes('small=false') || !line.includes('agent=build')) {
00127|       continue;
00128|     }
00129| 
00130|     const providerMatch = line.match(/providerID=([^\s]+)/);
00131|     const modelMatch = line.match(/modelID=([^\s]+)/);
00132|     const providerID = providerMatch?.[1];
00133|     const modelID = modelMatch?.[1];
00134|     if (providerID && modelID) {
00135|       observedModel = `${providerID}/${modelID}`;
00136|     }
00137|   }
00138| 
00139|   return observedModel;
00140| }
00141| 
00142| /**
00143|  * Extract the session id from the `--format json` event stream.
00144|  * Every emitted event carries a `sessionID` field.
00145|  * Preserved verbatim from the old adapter.
00146|  *
00147|  * @param {string|undefined} transcript
00148|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00149|  */
00150| export function extractSessionIdFromTranscript(transcript) {
00151|   if (!transcript) {
00152|     return undefined;
00153|   }
00154| 
00155|   for (const line of transcript.split('\n')) {
00156|     try {
00157|       const event = JSON.parse(line);
00158|       if (typeof event.sessionID === 'string' && event.sessionID) {
00159|         return event.sessionID;
00160|       }
00161|     } catch {
00162|       // Skip non-JSON lines
00163|     }
00164|   }
00165| 
00166|   return undefined;
00167| }
00168| 
00169| /**
00170|  * Extract the observed model from `opencode export <sessionID>` output.
00171|  * Assistant messages carry `providerID` and `modelID` in their info.
00172|  * Preserved verbatim from the old adapter.
00173|  *
00174|  * @param {string} exportOutput
00175|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00176|  */
00177| export function extractObservedModelFromSessionExport(exportOutput) {
00178|   const start = exportOutput.indexOf('{');
00179|   if (start === -1) {
00180|     return undefined;
00181|   }
00182| 
00183|   let parsed;
00184|   try {
00185|     parsed = JSON.parse(exportOutput.slice(start));
00186|   } catch {
00187|     return undefined;
00188|   }
00189| 
00190|   const messages = parsed.messages;
00191|   if (!Array.isArray(messages)) {
00192|     return undefined;
00193|   }
00194| 
00195|   for (const message of messages) {
00196|     const info = message.info;
00197|     if (info?.role !== 'assistant') {
00198|       continue;
00199|     }
00200|     if (
00201|       typeof info.providerID === 'string' && info.providerID &&
00202|       typeof info.modelID === 'string' && info.modelID
00203|     ) {
00204|       return `${info.providerID}/${info.modelID}`;
00205|     }
00206|   }
00207| 
00208|   return undefined;
00209| }
00210| 
00211| /**
00212|  * Run OpenCode over the workspace at `input.cwd` and return a RunnerResult.
00213|  *
00214|  * Auth (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and OPENCODE_ENABLE_EXA when web research is on)
00215|  * arrives via process.env — the orchestrator sets it on the `node run.mjs`
00216|  * invocation, and we pass process.env straight through to the CLI. The runner
00217|  * never handles secrets itself.
00218|  *
00219|  * @param {import('../plugin/contract.js').AgentRunInput} input
00220|  * @returns {Promise<import('../plugin/contract.js').RunnerResult>}
00221|  */
00222| export async function runAgent(input) {
00223|   const args = buildOpenCodeCliArgs(input);
00224| 
00225|   // spawnSync (not a shell string): the prompt is a plain argv element, so there
00226|   // is no shell quoting/escaping to get wrong. Blocking is fine — the runner has
00227|   // nothing else to do while the agent works. The sandbox-level timeout bounds it.
00228|   const res = spawnSync('opencode', args, {
00229|     cwd: input.cwd,
00230|     env: process.env,
00231|     encoding: 'utf8',
00232|     maxBuffer: 64 * 1024 * 1024,
00233|   });
00234| 
00235|   const stdout = res.stdout || '';
00236|   const stderr = res.stderr || '';
00237|   // Preserve the old concatenation order: stdout THEN stderr.
00238|   const output = stdout + stderr;
00239|   // spawnSync sets status=null + error when the binary can't be spawned at all.
00240|   const agentExitCode = res.status == null ? -1 : res.status;
00241| 
00242|   // Capture the transcript from the combined output (old: over stdout+stderr).
00243|   const transcript = extractTranscriptFromOutput(output) ?? null;
00244| 
00245|   // Resolve the model OpenCode actually used. The `--format json` events never
00246|   // include it, so first try scraping the printed logs (works on OpenCode <=
00247|   // 1.16.x), then fall back to `opencode export <sessionID>`, whose assistant
00248|   // messages carry providerID/modelID (OpenCode 1.17.0 changed the log format,
00249|   // which broke the scrape). Observation must never fail the run.
00250|   let observedModel = extractObservedModelFromOpenCodeOutput(output);
00251|   if (!observedModel) {
00252|     const sessionId = extractSessionIdFromTranscript(transcript ?? undefined);
00253|     if (sessionId) {
00254|       try {
00255|         const exportRes = spawnSync('opencode', ['export', sessionId], {
00256|           cwd: input.cwd,
00257|           env: process.env,
00258|           encoding: 'utf8',
00259|           maxBuffer: 64 * 1024 * 1024,
00260|         });
00261|         if ((exportRes.status == null ? -1 : exportRes.status) === 0) {
00262|           observedModel = extractObservedModelFromSessionExport(exportRes.stdout || '');
00263|         }
00264|       } catch {
00265|         // Leave observedModel undefined.
00266|       }
00267|     }
00268|   }
00269|   const observedModelOrNull = normalizeObservedModel(observedModel, input) ?? null;
00270| 
00271|   if (res.error || agentExitCode !== 0) {
00272|     // Mirror the old error string: last 5 lines of output, else a coded fallback.
00273|     const errorLines = output.trim().split('\n').slice(-5).join('\n');
00274|     const fallback = res.error
00275|       ? `Failed to run opencode: ${res.error.message}`
00276|       : `OpenCode CLI exited with code ${agentExitCode}`;
00277|     return {
00278|       ok: false,
00279|       output,
00280|       transcript,
00281|       observedModel: observedModelOrNull,
00282|       error: errorLines || fallback,
00283|       agentExitCode,
00284|     };
00285|   }
00286| 
00287|   return {
00288|     ok: true,
00289|     output,
00290|     transcript,
00291|     observedModel: observedModelOrNull,
00292|     error: null,
00293|     agentExitCode,
00294|   };
00295| }
00296| 
00297| /* ─────────────────────────── runnable (CLI) entry ─────────────────────────── */
00298| 
00299| // True when this file is executed directly (`node run.mjs ...`), false when imported.
00300| const isMain = process.argv[1] && fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) === process.argv[1];
00301| 
00302| if (isMain) {
00303|   // argv[2] is the AgentRunInput JSON (never contains secrets).
00304|   const input = JSON.parse(process.argv[2]);
00305| 
00306|   // Always produce a RunnerResult, even if the runner itself throws, so the host
00307|   // always has a result file to read (node exit code stays 0 except on a truly
00308|   // unrecoverable crash before we can write).
00309|   let result;
00310|   try {
00311|     result = await runAgent(input);
00312|   } catch (e) {
00313|     result = {
00314|       ok: false,
00315|       output: '',
00316|       transcript: null,
00317|       observedModel: null,
00318|       error: e && e.message ? e.message : String(e),
00319|       agentExitCode: -1,
00320|     };
00321|   }
00322| 
00323|   // Source of truth: the result file the host reads back via sandbox.readFile.
00324|   try {
00325|     mkdirSync(dirname(input.resultPath), { recursive: true });
00326|     writeFileSync(input.resultPath, JSON.stringify(result));
00327|   } catch {
00328|     // If the file can't be written, the host falls back to the marker line below.
00329|   }
00330| 
00331|   // Fallback channel: a compact status line (no transcript — it can be huge).
00332|   process.stdout.write(
00333|     '__AGENT_RESULT__ ' +
00334|       JSON.stringify({
00335|         ok: result.ok,
00336|         observedModel: result.observedModel,
00337|         error: result.error,
00338|         agentExitCode: result.agentExitCode,
00339|       }) +
00340|       '\n'
00341|   );
00342| 
00343|   // Exit 0: "the runner ran". Agent success/failure is conveyed via result.ok, not
00344|   // the node exit code (the host distinguishes the two).
00345|   process.exit(0);
00346| }

/**
 * OpenCode in-sandbox runner.
 *
 * This file is shipped INTO the sandbox by the orchestrator and executed there as
 * `node __agent_eval__/run.mjs '<AgentRunInput JSON>'`. It is intentionally
 * ZERO-DEPENDENCY (only `node:*` builtins) because the sandbox only has the
 * fixture's own deps + the installed `opencode` CLI — it cannot import anything
 * from the @vercel/agent-eval package.
 *
 * Dual mode:
 *   - runnable: invoked directly → reads argv, runs the agent, writes the result
 *     file + prints a status line, exits 0.
 *   - importable: `import { runAgent } from './run.mjs'` → returns a RunnerResult
 *     (no file write, no exit). This is what a future in-sandbox judge reuses.
 *
 * The pure helpers below are exported (not just `runAgent`) so they can be
 * unit-tested directly — the same code the sandbox runs (see opencode.test.ts).
 */

<file>
00001| ---
00002| title: Adopting Partial Prefetching
00003| nav_title: Adopting Partial Prefetching
00004| description: Learn how to enable Partial Prefetching and what changes for `<Link>`.
00005| related:
00006|   title: Next Steps
00007|   description: Learn more about prefetching and instant navigations.
00008|   links:
00009|     - app/guides/instant-navigation
00010|     - app/guides/optimizing-prefetching
00011|     - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching
00012|     - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/prefetch
00013|     - app/api-reference/functions/prefetch
00014|     - app/api-reference/functions/navigation
00015| ---
00016| 
00017| [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prefetching) changes what a `<Link>` downloads for a Cache Components route. With Partial Prefetching enabled, a `<Link>` prefetches the route's [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell): its static content and the cached content that doesn't depend on the URL. Next.js builds one App Shell per route and reuses it for every link to that route, rather than prefetching each link separately as it did before.
00018| 
00019| To prefetch more than the App Shell, a link can opt into [per-link prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) with [`<Link prefetch={true}>`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#prefetch). The prefetch can then resolve cached URL-specific content that depends on `params`, `searchParams`, or the full URL.
00020| 
00021| Along the way, Next.js surfaces [instant navigation](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) insights in development, naming the link or route to change.
00022| 
00023| > **Good to know**: Partial Prefetching only works when [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled.
00024| 
00025| ## Use the adoption skill (recommended)
00026| 
00027| The [`next-partial-prefetching-adoption`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/skills/next-partial-prefetching-adoption) skill drives this adoption with a coding agent. It reviews your `<Link prefetch={true}>` calls, captures the prefetched UI to preserve with [`instant()` tests](#verify-prefetched-ui-with-tests) when a production test rig is available, then enables the flag and checks each route for the insights this guide covers.
00028| 
00029| Install the skill:
00030| 
00031| ```bash filename="Terminal"
00032| npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-partial-prefetching-adoption
00033| ```
00034| 
00035| Then give the agent this prompt:
00036| 
00037| ```prompt
00038| Adopt Partial Prefetching in this project using the next-partial-prefetching-adoption skill.
00039| ```
00040| 
00041| ## Or adopt by hand
00042| 
00043| To adopt an existing app by hand:
00044| 
00045| 1. [Review existing full prefetches](#migrate-existing-full-prefetches) and choose which part of each destination should continue to be prefetched. You can use [`instant()` tests](#verify-prefetched-ui-with-tests) to add regression coverage.
00046| 2. [Enable `partialPrefetching`](#enable-partial-prefetching). For larger migrations, you can [adopt incrementally](#adopting-incrementally) with the global flag off. [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prefetching) changes what a `<Link>` downloads for a Cache Components route. With Partial Prefetching enabled, a `<Link>` prefetches the route's [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell): its static content and the cached content that doesn't depend on the URL. Next.js builds one App Shell per route and reuses it for every link to that route, rather than prefetching each link separately as it did before.

To prefetch more than the App Shell, a link can opt into [per-link prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) with [`<Link prefetch={true}>`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#prefetch). The prefetch can then resolve cached URL-specific content that depends on `params`, `searchParams`, or the full URL.

With Partial Prefetching enabled, a `<Link>` prefetches the route's [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell): its static content and the cached content that doesn't depend on the URL. Next.js builds one App Shell per route and reuses it for every link to that route, rather than prefetching each link separately as it did before.

To prefetch more than the App Shell, a link can opt into [per-link prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) with [`<Link prefetch={true}>`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#prefetch). The prefetch can then resolve cached URL-specific content that depends on `params`, `searchParams`, or the full URL.

00282| | [Delivers real-time content that must stay fresh per request](#real-time-content) | Remove `prefetch={true}` and let the content stream in.                   |

  route: string,
  missingFiles: readonly string[]
): Error {
  let message = `Route "${route}": Could not validate that a segment in your UI has instant navigation.`
  if (missingFiles.length > 0) {
    const label =
      missingFiles.length === 1 ? 'Dropped segment' : 'Dropped segments'
    message +=
      `\n\nThis segment was dropped from rendering. Issues that would prevent instant navigation will go undetected.` +
      `\n\n${label}:\n${missingFiles.map((p) => `  ${p}`).join('\n')}` +
      `\n\nWays to fix this:` +
      `\n  - [render] Render the dropped segment` +
      `\n  - [ignore] Set \`export const instant = false\` to opt the dropped segment out of instant-navigation validation` +
      `\n\nLearn more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/instant-unrendered-segment`
  }
  return new Error(message)
}

export function createLinkPrefetchPartialError(pathname: string): Error {
  return new Error(
    `Next.js encountered dynamic data during prefetching for "${pathname}".\n\n` +
      `This will lead to slower, more expensive prefetches.\n\n` +
      `Ways to fix this:\n` +
      `  - [upgrade] Opt into Partial Prefetching by exporting \`const prefetch = 'partial'\` from the page or layout, or by setting \`partialPrefetching: true\` in next.config to opt the whole app in\n` +
      `  - [disable] Remove \`prefetch={true}\` from the <Link> to use the default prefetch\n` +
      `  - [ignore] Set \`export const instant = false\` to opt the route out of instant-navigation validation\n\n` +
      `Learn more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/instant-link-prefetch-partial`
  )
}

metadata.preview:
### Client Component Pages

A soft navigation into a page with `"use client"` at the top behaves like a single-page app transition, with no server render at navigation time, which makes it instant. The dev overlay doesn't include this in its fix cards because it has bigger implications than the recommended approaches, which keep the page in the server-component model. Reach for `"use client"` when the page is fully interactive and must be a client component.

> **Good to know**: `"use client"` doesn't skip validation for the static shell. Hooks like `useSearchParams()` still need a `<Suspense>` boundary.

## Visualize loading states with the Next.js DevTools

As you develop a route, the Next.js DevTools let you see what your users see on page loads and client navigations before dynamic data streams in. Use it to verify that your loading states look right, confirm the content you expect appears immediately, and iterate on where to place `<Suspense>` boundaries.

The [React DevTools Suspense panel](https://react.dev/learn/react-developer-tools) complements this: it lists the `<Suspense>` boundaries in the tree and lets you toggle each one between its fallback and resolved state, so you can see exactly which boundary covers which part of the page.

{/* TODO: screenshot — React DevTools Suspense panel listing boundaries with toggle controls */}

The Navigation Inspector is available when Cache Components is enabled:

metadata.preview:
### Client Component Pages

A soft navigation into a page with `"use client"` at the top behaves like a single-page app transition, with no server render at navigation time, which makes it instant. The dev overlay doesn't include this in its fix cards because it has bigger implications than the recommended approaches, which keep the page in the server-component model. Reach for `"use client"` when the page is fully interactive and must be a client component.

> **Good to know**: `"use client"` doesn't skip validation for the static shell. Hooks like `useSearchParams()` still need a `<Suspense>` boundary.

## Visualize loading states with the Next.js DevTools

As you develop a route, the Next.js DevTools let you see what your users see on page loads and client navigations before dynamic data streams in. Use it to verify that your loading states look right, confirm the content you expect appears immediately, and iterate on where to place `<Suspense>` boundaries.

The [React DevTools Suspense panel](https://react.dev/learn/react-developer-tools) complements this: it lists the `<Suspense>` boundaries in the tree and lets you toggle each one between its fallback and resolved state, so you can see exactly which boundary covers which part of the page.

{/* TODO: screenshot — React DevTools Suspense panel listing boundaries with toggle controls */}

The Navigation Inspector is available when Cache Components is enabled:
